clinicalPearls: The most common Ehlers-Danlos subtype, yet it remains a clinical diagnosis as no confirmatory gene has been identified.

Diagnosis uses the current consensus criteria requiring generalised joint hypermobility together with systemic features, a positive family history and/or musculoskeletal complications, and exclusion of other disorders.
Chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain, recurrent joint subluxation and dislocation and frequent soft-tissue injuries dominate the clinical picture.
Common associated problems include orthostatic intolerance and postural tachycardia, functional gastrointestinal disorders, fatigue, anxiety and mast cell activation symptoms.
Skin may be mildly soft or hyperextensible but lacks the atrophic scarring that characterises classical EDS.
Generalised joint hypermobility is assessed with the Beighton score, interpreted against age, sex and pubertal status.
Other heritable connective tissue disorders such as Marfan, vascular EDS and classical EDS must be excluded before the diagnosis is made.
Management is multidisciplinary, centred on graded physiotherapy, joint protection, pain management and treatment of autonomic and gastrointestinal comorbidities.
reference.pathophysiology: The molecular basis of hypermobile EDS is unknown and the condition is presumed to be genetically heterogeneous rather than caused by a single gene, which is why no confirmatory test exists. The clinical phenotype is attributed to a generalised abnormality of connective tissue that reduces the tensile integrity and proprioceptive feedback of ligaments, tendons, joint capsules and fascia, producing ligamentous laxity, joint instability and a tendency to soft-tissue injury. Altered connective tissue and autonomic regulation are thought to underlie the frequently associated dysautonomia, gastrointestinal dysmotility and pain amplification, although these mechanisms remain incompletely defined and inheritance most often appears autosomal dominant with variable expression.
additionalDifferentials: Fibromyalgia and chronic widespread pain syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Beighton scoring and structured application of the consensus diagnostic criteria
Genetic testing to exclude other heritable connective tissue disorders
Echocardiography to exclude aortic root involvement
Autonomic assessment such as active stand or tilt-table testing where indicated
Assessment for gastrointestinal, mast cell and psychological comorbidities
Physiotherapy and functional evaluation of joint stability and proprioception
redFlags: Features suggesting aortic or arterial disease that should prompt reclassification to another subtype
An arterial rupture or dissection event
Marked skin fragility with atrophic scarring more typical of classical or other subtypes
Severe, refractory orthostatic symptoms with syncope
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal. However, chronic pain, fatigue, joint instability and autonomic and gastrointestinal symptoms can substantially impair function and quality of life over time.
pitfalls: Over-diagnosis in people who have joint hypermobility but do not meet the full consensus criteria.
Missing aortic pathology or another heritable connective tissue disorder by omitting cardiac imaging and genetic exclusion.
Dismissing autonomic, gastrointestinal and pain symptoms as purely functional without appropriate assessment.
Conflating isolated generalised hypermobility, which is common and often asymptomatic, with the full syndrome.
